'''Lillian Eva Quan Dyck''', {{post-nominals|country=CAN|OC}} (born August 24, 1945) is a retired Canadian [[Senate of Canada|senator]] from [[Saskatchewan]]. A member of the [[Cree]] [[Gordon First Nation]] in Saskatchewan, and a first generation Chinese Canadian, she is the first female First Nations senator and first Canadian-born senator of Chinese descent.<ref name=":1" />

Before being appointed to the Senate, Dyck was a [[neuroscientist]] with the [[University of Saskatchewan]], where she was also an associate dean. On March 12, 1999, Dyck, who is one of the first [[Aboriginal peoples in Canada|Aboriginal]] women in Canada to pursue an academic career in the sciences, was presented with a [[Indspire Awards|lifetime achievement award]] by [[Indspire]]. She continues to teach at the university as well as conduct research on a part-time basis. In 2019 she received a Women of Distinction Awards Lifetime Achievement Award from the [[YWCA]] Saskatoon.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatoon/senator-lillian-dyck-lifetime-achievement-award|title=Senator Lillian Dyck to receive lifetime achievement award|date=2019-05-06|work=CBC News Saskatoon|access-date=2019-08-31}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ywcasaskatoon.com/about-the-ywca/women-of-distinction/2019-women-of-distinction-recipients/|title=2019 Women of Distinction Recipients|website=YWCA Saskatoon|language=en-CA|access-date=2019-08-31|archive-date=2020-11-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101135913/https://www.ywcasaskatoon.com/about-the-ywca/women-of-distinction/2019-women-of-distinction-recipients/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Alongside her research and academic work, the Honourable Dr. Lillian Eva Quan Dyck is well known for advocating for equity in the education and employment of women, Chinese Canadians and Aboriginals.

== Early life and education ==
Dyck was born in [[North Battleford]], Saskatchewan, to a Chinese father, Yok Lee Quan, and [[Cree]] mother, Eva Muriel Mcnab. Her father came to Canada after paying the [[Chinese head tax in Canada|Head Tax]], leaving his first family behind in China. Her mother was born on the [[Gordon 86|Gordon Reserve]], but lost her status when she married a non-Indian. She, like most First Nations women at the time, was sent to a [[Canadian Indian residential school system|residential school]].

Dyck moved around frequently, living in many small towns in Saskatchewan and Alberta.  Her family hid their Indigenous heritage in order to protect themselves from racism. Taking her father's last name of Quan, her family was essentially the only Chinese family in town.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sencanada.ca/en/sencaplus/people/from-cafe-daughter-to-senator-dy-story-of-struggle-and-identity-takes-the-stage-at-the-nac/|title=Senate of Canada - From 'Café Daughter' to senator: The story of Lillian Eva Dyck takes the stage at the NAC|last=Canada|first=Senate of|website=Senate of Canada|date=16 June 2017|language=en-CA|access-date=2018-09-22}}</ref> As most First Nations people were living on reserves, she had no connection to them. Her family was the only non-white family in town.

Her father ran a Chinese cafe.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://sen.parl.gc.ca/ldyck/html/eng/editedScience%20to%20the%20Senate%20-%20EDMONTON%202017.pdf|title=My story: An Aboriginal Neuroscientist and Senator|last=Dyck|first=Lillian|date=April 2017|access-date=September 22, 2018|archive-date=June 14, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170614131151/http://sen.parl.gc.ca/ldyck/html/eng/editedScience%20to%20the%20Senate%20-%20EDMONTON%202017.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> She grew up waitressing and doing many other jobs, such as at the Regal Cafe in [[Killam, Alberta]], where her mother's tombstone lies.<ref name=":2" />

Dyck attended Swift Current Collegiate Institute, where she was actively encouraged to go to university.

Dyck earned her Bachelor of Arts (Honours), Master of Science Degrees in Biochemistry in 1968 and 1970 respectively, as well as her Ph.D. in Biological Psychiatry in 1981, all from the University of Saskatchewan. She was conferred a Doctor of Letters, Honoris Causa by [[Cape Breton University]] in 2007.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://sencanada.ca/en/senators/dyck-lillian-eva/|title=Senate of Canada - Senator Lillian Eva Dyck|last=Canada|first=Senate of|website=Senate of Canada|date=11 October 2016|language=en-CA|access-date=2018-09-22}}</ref>

== Career ==
=== Academic ===
Before being appointed to the Senate, Dyck was a [[neuroscientist]] with the [[University of Saskatchewan]], where she was also associate dean. On March 12, 1999, Dyck, who is of [[Cree]] and [[Chinese Canadian|Chinese]] heritage and was one of the first [[Aboriginal peoples in Canada|Aboriginal]] women in Canada to pursue an academic career in the sciences, was presented with a [[Indspire Awards|lifetime achievement award]] by [[Indspire]]. Her research focuses on mechanisms of action of [[monoamine oxidase inhibitor]]s to identify drugs useful for treatment of [[neurological disorder]]s and [[stroke]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ammsa.com/publications/windspeaker/brother-encouraged-students-curiosity-about-science-0|title=Brother encouraged 'A' student's curiosity about science|website=Ammsa.com|language=en|access-date=2018-09-22}}</ref> She continues to teach at the university as well as conduct research on a part-time basis.

=== Senate ===
Dyck was appointed to the Senate on the recommendation of [[Prime Minister of Canada|Prime Minister]] [[Paul Martin]] on March 24, 2005.

Upon appointment, Dyck wished to sit as a [[New Democratic Party (Canada)|New Democratic Party]] senator, but NDP spokesperson [[Karl Belanger]] immediately indicated that the party would not recognize her as a member of the NDP [[caucus]]: as the party platform specifically favours abolition of the Senate, it refused to confer legitimacy on the body by accepting Dyck; additionally, Dyck's membership in the NDP was revealed to have lapsed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/dallaire-eggleton-among-9-new-senators-1.566394|title=Dallaire, Eggleton among 9 new senators|date=March 24, 2005|publisher=CBC News|accessdate=2015-11-18}}</ref> Under the rules of the Senate, senators are free to designate themselves however they see fit, and Dyck changed her designation to say ''Independent New Democratic Party''.<ref>[http://www2.parl.gc.ca/Parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e6ec2251-b539-401f-bf63-7becb4c5528f&Language=E Parliament of Canada—DYCK, The Hon. Lillian Eva]</ref> On January 15, 2009, she joined the [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal]] Senate caucus.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/2009/01/15/independent_senator_jumps_to_liberals.html|title=Independent senator jumps to Liberals|date=January 15, 2009|work=[[Toronto Star]]|accessdate=2015-11-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://sen.parl.gc.ca/ldyck/html/eng/01home.html |title=Official Site for Senator Lillian Dyck |access-date=2008-08-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081004182432/http://sen.parl.gc.ca/ldyck/html/eng/01home.html |archive-date=2008-10-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On January 29, 2014, Liberal Party leader [[Justin Trudeau]] announced all Liberal Senators, including Dyck, were removed from the Liberal caucus, and would continue sitting as Independents.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/justin-trudeau-removes-senators-from-liberal-caucus-1.2515273|title=Justin Trudeau removes senators from Liberal caucus|date=January 29, 2014|publisher=CBC News|accessdate=2015-11-18}}</ref> The Senators referred to themselves as the [[Senate Liberal Caucus]] even though they are no longer members of the parliamentary Liberal caucus.<ref name="expuls">{{cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/trudeau-to-boot-senators-from-liberal-caucus-in-bid-to-restore-senate-independence/article16567413/|title=Trudeau's expulsion catches Liberal senators by surprise|date=January 29, 2014|newspaper=Globe and Mail|accessdate=January 29, 2014}}</ref>

In 2014 Dyck accused Conservative MP [[Rob Clarke (politician)|Rob Clarke]], who is also native, of "behaving like a white man" by pushing the [[Indian Act]] Amendment and Replacement Act. She later said she recognized the comment could be hurtful.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/rob-clarke-s-controversial-bill-to-change-the-indian-act-passed-into-law-1.2881801|title=Rob Clarke's controversial bill to change the Indian Act passed into law|date=December 22, 2014|publisher=CBC News|accessdate=2015-11-18}}</ref>

In April 2018 [http://fafia-afai.org/en/ The Feminist Alliance for International Action] recognized Lillian as a member of [[the Indigenous Famous Six]]. Other members are Jeannette Corbiere-Lavell, Yvonne Bedard, Sharon McIvor, Lynn Gehl, and Senator Sandra Lovelace Nicholas.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://windspeaker.com/news/windspeaker-news/famous-six-to-be-celebrated-for-work-on-61a-all-the-way|title = 'Famous Six' to be celebrated for work on '6(1)a All the Way'}}</ref>

In November 2019, Dyck joined the rest of the [[Senate Liberal Caucus]] in deciding to dissolve the caucus and form the new [[Progressive Senate Group]].<ref name="new-senate-can-faction-14nov2019">{{cite news |last1=Tasker |first1=John Paul (J.P.) |title=There's another new faction in the Senate: the Progressive Senate Group |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/new-faction-progressive-senate-group-1.5358269 |accessdate=14 November 2019 |publisher=CBC News Online |date=14 November 2019}}</ref><ref name="one-time-lib-senators-progressive-senate-group-14nov2019">{{cite news |title=One-time Liberal senators rename themselves as Progressive Senate Group |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/article/one-time-liberal-senators-rename-themselves-as-progressive-senate-group/ |access-date=14 November 2019 |agency=The Canadian Press |publisher=CTV News |date=14 November 2019}}</ref>

==== Political work ====
Dyck's priorities as a senator included Aboriginal women (Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women, Violence towards Aboriginal Women), Bill C-31 and its impact on Aboriginal women and men, women in science (recruitment and retention of women into professional scientific and technological careers), Aboriginal education and employment (recruitment and retention of aboriginals in the educational system and on the job), and mental health (the causes and treatment of psychiatric disorders).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sen.parl.gc.ca/ldyck/html/eng/04senate.html|title=Senator Lillian Dyck|website=sen.parl.gc.ca|access-date=2018-09-22|archive-date=2018-09-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180925040440/http://sen.parl.gc.ca/ldyck/html/eng/04senate.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=APTN News|title=Discrepancy when men are sentenced for violence against Indigenous women {{!}} APTN News|date=28 November 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHtxQUoMhJI|access-date=2018-12-31}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.parl.ca/LegisInfo/BillDetails.aspx?billId=8067395&Language=E|title=LEGISinfo - Senate Public Bill S-215 (42-1)|website=www.parl.ca|access-date=2018-12-31}}</ref>

She was outspoken on the issue of [[violence against women]] and successfully advocated for changes to legislation that will require judges to consider stiffer penalties for violent crimes against Indigenous women.<ref name="Retirement">{{cite news |title=Sask. Senator Lillian Dyck announces retirement after serving more than 15 years |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatoon/lillian-dyck-announces-retirement-1.5699055 |accessdate=August 25, 2020 |work=CBC News |date=August 25, 2020}}</ref>

She also worked on Bill S-3, a bill that aimed to restore official Indian status for thousands of women who lost their status for marrying non-indigenous men.<ref name="Retirement"/>

== Works inspired by her ==
''Café Daughter'', a play written by [[Kenneth T. Williams]], was a fictionalized account of Dyck's childhood.<ref>Colin Maclean, [https://edmontonsun.com/2015/11/27/colin-maclean-review-cafe-daughter "Colin MacLean review: Cafe Daughter"]. ''[[Edmonton Sun]]'', November 27, 2015.</ref> The play was adapted into the 2023 film ''[[Café Daughter]]'' by Mohawk filmmaker [[Shelley Niro]].<ref>Eden Suh, [https://www.sudbury.com/local-news/film-cafe-daughter-shooting-wraps-up-in-sudbury-5396092 "Film: Café Daughter shooting wraps up in Sudbury"]. ''[[Sudbury.com]]'', May 22, 2022.</ref>
